justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a mildly bullish drift assumption across all three horizons. For the one-day estimate, I anchored close to the prevailing market level with only a small upward nudge, reflecting the tendency of equity indices to exhibit slight positive drift on any given day while acknowledging that short-term momentum and overnight futures positioning can create small directional biases. The one-week estimate steps up modestly, consistent with the historical annualized return of broad equity markets translating into a small weekly expected gain. The one-month estimate continues this gentle upward trajectory, reflecting the long-run positive equity risk premium while remaining humble about the many crosscurrents that can affect markets over a four-week window.

The confidence interval widths are primarily driven by the well-established scaling of volatility with the square root of time. At the one-day horizon, realized volatility in major equity indices typically runs in the range of 1–1.5% per day, which produces a relatively tight band. By one week, compounding uncertainty widens the interval considerably, and by one month the interval nearly triples in half-width compared to the daily case. The asymmetry in intervals is intentional — equity distributions tend to have fatter left tails due to the potential for sharp drawdowns, so downside bounds are set somewhat more conservatively than pure symmetry would suggest.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals include a sudden shift in Federal Reserve policy communication, an unexpected inflation print, or a geopolitical shock that triggers a risk-off flight. On the upside, a surprisingly strong earnings season, a ceasefire in an active conflict, or an unanticipated dovish pivot could generate a sharp rally beyond the upper bounds. Liquidity conditions also matter — if market depth deteriorates quickly, moves can overshoot what historical volatility alone would predict.

It is worth emphasizing that even well-calibrated intervals at 90% confidence will be violated roughly one time in ten, and financial markets are prone to tail events that cluster in ways that make even that frequency optimistic during stress periods. The one-month interval in particular should be treated with appropriate skepticism, as a single unexpected macro development in any given week could render the entire range obsolete within days.
